name: Fatima Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working week look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a violinist, so the week is a patchwork. Tuesday and Thursday afternoons I teach at the community music school on Mill Street, mostly kids between eight and fourteen. Most Saturdays I play weddings with the Linden Quartet, and every few weeks I get called to Harbour Lane Studios to play strings on someone's pop record. I love the teaching and the weddings, but the travel and the late nights wear me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the money come together across all that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Teaching is the steady part, about a third of what I earn, paid by the school every month. Weddings are the best money per hour but they bunch up between May and September, so winter is thin. The studio sessions are a bonus, maybe four hundred a month when they come. I've got about three months of rent and bills saved, and my partner Jonas is a nurse, so between us we're fine as long as nothing big goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say I told you so, to be honest. Half my musician friends have been panicking about AI music for two years, and I've been saying people still want a real person playing at their wedding. I'd put something on the musicians' union group chat saying we should still push for proper rules, because the hype was used to scare us into cheaper fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my life wouldn't change much, and that's not the same as it being easy. Winter is still thin, rent on our flat went up eighty a month in September, and my violin needs a new bridge and a rehair that'll cost about three hundred. A plateau doesn't fix the fact that every January I count weddings booked for summer and do sums on the back of a setlist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I do: the two teaching afternoons, the quartet, the studio when they call. I'd try to get one more teaching afternoon at Mill Street from January, because that's the money that turns up in winter. I'd also keep paying my union dues and go to the spring meeting about session rates, which I usually skip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly, but the relief has a limit. I'd still be watching the bank account every February. It's a low hum of worry I've had since I left college, and AI being hype doesn't switch it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the routine tasks AI does take over. Is any of your work like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio work, a bit. Harbour Lane already uses a program to tidy up timing on string parts, so they need fewer takes and book me for three hours instead of four. That's an hour's pay gone, every session, and nobody asked me. If even a plateau shaves bits like that, it adds up over a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you worry about first in a bad winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, always, because it's the biggest and Jonas and I split it down the middle. I'd skip the bridge and rehair before I'd ask Jonas to cover my half. I'd rather play on a tired bow for a few more months than feel like I'm being carried.

say: I'd say **real musicians** were right not to panic about AI music.
I'd post that the hype was used to push **fees down** and we still need rules.
think: My life stays the same, and that includes **thin winters** and rising rent.
Even small AI tidying at the studio already cut **one hour** from each session booking.
do: Ask Mill Street for a **third teaching afternoon** starting in January.
Go to the **union meeting** on session rates in spring instead of skipping it.
feel: **Relieved**, but the usual low hum of **money worry** stays.
S0.quote: A plateau doesn't fix the fact that every January I count weddings booked for summer and do sums on the back of a setlist.
fieldNote: Freelance pattern drives her worry more than AI: **summer weddings** carry a thin winter.
She noticed AI already trimming **studio bookings** by an hour and resents not being asked.
Pride shows in refusing to let **Jonas cover** her half of the rent.

steps.text: Ask Mill Street music school for a third teaching afternoon in January
Attend the union's spring meeting on studio session rates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the union says: if a company trains a program on recordings of people like me, it should pay us and ask us first. I'd share the petitions and turn up to the protest outside the streaming office if there was one. I'm not going to pretend it's progress when it's just taking our work for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the studio work goes first. Producers will type in what they want and get a string section in ten minutes, so Harbour Lane will stop calling me. Wedding couples might start booking apps and planning tools, but they'll still want four people in black playing Pachelbel as the bride walks in. Teaching is in the middle, because parents might try a cheap AI violin app before they pay for lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop counting on studio money at all and build the budget around teaching and weddings. I'd ask the quartet to raise our wedding fee by ten percent before the season fills, while couples still book us. I'd go to every union meeting that year and help with the campaign for payment when recordings are used to train these programs. I won't start using the AI apps myself, I just won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry more than scared, I think. It feels like someone walked into my house and took the furniture, and then told me I'm old-fashioned for minding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if parents at Mill Street start switching to an app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd lose students slowly, one or two a term, and I'd notice it in my payslip by summer. A few parents already ask if their kid can just learn from videos. I tell them a video can't fix how a ten-year-old holds the bow, but if an app can watch through the camera and correct them, some will go for it because it's cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't use AI tools yourself. Is there any version where you would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if the union negotiated something fair and the people who made the recordings got paid. Until then it feels like crossing a picket line. I'd rather lose the studio work than help a program that learned to play violin from my friends' recordings without paying them.

say: I'd say companies must **ask and pay** musicians before training on our recordings.
I'd share **union petitions** and join any protest outside the streaming firms.
think: **Studio work** goes first because producers can type in a string section.
Weddings stay human, but **lesson numbers** may slip to cheap violin apps.
do: Drop studio money from the budget and plan around **teaching and weddings**.
Push the quartet for a **ten percent** rise in wedding fees.
Join the union **training-pay campaign** and attend every meeting that year.
feel: Mostly **angry**, like someone took her things and called her **old-fashioned**.
S1.quote: I'd rather lose the studio work than help a program that learned to play violin from my friends' recordings without paying them.
fieldNote: Her refusal to use AI is **moral**, not just habit: she compares it to crossing a picket line.
She sees the **studio loss** clearly and expects a slow drip of students leaving.
Her plan leans on **collective action** more than on changing her own work.

steps.text: Raise the Linden Quartet's wedding fee by ten percent before next season
Rebuild the monthly budget without any studio session income
Join the union campaign for pay when recordings train AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need governments to step in now, not after it's happened. I'd be at every march and I'd write to my representative about a tax on these companies to fund artists and teachers. Online I'd be the angry violinist, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose most of my teaching within a year or two, because a perfect patient tutor in every kid's tablet is hard to argue against when it costs almost nothing. Weddings might hold on until the robots come around 2031, and even then I can't picture a robot quartet at a wedding. Two years isn't enough time for me to become anything else, so I'd be hanging on to the weddings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop every non-essential spend straight away: no new bow, no holiday, cancel the streaming services. I'd try to build my savings from three months to six by playing more weddings, even the cheap midweek ones I usually turn down. I'd sign up for the union's hardship fund and ask about any government support for artists. And I'd be in the streets about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. I've only ever been a violinist. Jonas keeps saying nurses will be fine, and I'm glad, but I don't want to be the one who's carried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the hands-on part of your work when the robots come three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part I'm hoping buys me time. Playing in a room, reading the couple's faces, stretching the processional when the bride is late, that's all hands and ears. But if teaching and studio work are gone by 2028, three extra years of wedding money is something to hold on to while things get sorted, not a whole living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas the night it really sank in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm scared I wasted twenty years practising something nobody needs. He'd tell me that's rubbish, and then we'd sit down with the spreadsheet he keeps. I'd probably ask whether we could stay in the flat on his salary alone if it came to that.

say: I'd say governments must act **now**, with a **tax** on AI firms for artists.
I'd be at every **march** and writing to my representative.
think: **Teaching** could mostly vanish within a year or two to free AI tutors.
Weddings may last until **2031**, but that's time to hold on, not a living.
do: Cut **all extras** at once: streaming, holidays and the new bow.
Grow savings from three to **six months** by taking cheap midweek weddings.
Apply to the union **hardship fund** and any government artist support.
feel: **Frightened** that twenty years of practice might now be worthless.
Uneasy about being **carried** by Jonas's nursing salary.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough time for me to become anything else, so I'd be hanging on to the weddings.
fieldNote: She expects to lose **most of her income** fast and has no other trade to fall back on.
The three-year robot gap matters to her only as a **bridge** of wedding work.
Her strongest fear is personal: becoming **dependent** on her partner.

steps.text: Cancel streaming services, holiday plans and the new bow purchase
Take midweek weddings to build savings to six months
Apply to the union hardship fund and artist support schemes
Write to her representative about taxing AI firms for artists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, but with a bit more time to organise. I'd say we've got five years to get laws in place that protect musicians and teachers, so let's not waste them. I'd want the union to have a plan, not just a statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough that I can't pretend it won't happen, but short enough that I couldn't retrain into anything big. I think I'd lose teaching around 2030, and the studio work long before that. Weddings would carry me through to about 2034, if couples still care about a real quartet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get more involved in the union, maybe a branch rep role, because I'd rather be in the room where deals get made. I'd put an extra hundred a month into savings and stop eating out. I'd also look at a part-time job in music therapy at the hospital where Jonas works, because that's people in a room, and I'd want to talk to someone there before 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less trapped than the two-year one. There's a road there, even if I don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Music therapy needs more training. Would you actually do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a two-year course and I hate the idea of going back to being a student at thirty. But I've seen what a violin does for someone on a ward who can't speak. If the choice was that or nothing, I'd do it, slowly and grumbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union rep job to win?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fee every time a musician's recording is used to train these programs, and a fund for teachers who lose students. The union is the only place where a violinist like me has any voice against companies worth more than whole countries.

say: I'd say there are **five years** to pass laws protecting musicians and teachers.
I'd ask the union for a real **plan**, not just a statement.
think: **Teaching** probably goes around 2030 and studio work well before that.
Weddings might carry her to **2034**, if couples still value a live quartet.
do: Stand for **branch rep** in the musicians' union.
Save an extra **hundred a month** and stop eating out.
Ask about **music therapy** work at the hospital where Jonas works.
feel: **Anxious**, though **less trapped** than in the two-year picture.
S3.quote: The union is the only place where a violinist like me has any voice against companies worth more than whole countries.
fieldNote: Even with five years she expects to lose **teaching and studio** income, most of her earnings.
She'd consider **music therapy** only reluctantly, framing it as the last option.
Her faith in the **union** is strong and sits at the centre of her plans.

steps.text: Stand for musicians' union branch rep at the next election
Save an extra hundred a month by cutting meals out
Ask the hospital's therapy team about music therapy training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly if governments want to. Fund music teachers, pay artists when their work trains these programs, and give people time to move. I'd say it at the union and I'd say it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is my whole thirties. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, and I think the teaching and studio work would be long gone by then. Weddings would still be there until near the end, and maybe after, because I really can't see couples choosing a robot for that moment. I'd have time to train as a music therapist and still play on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep everything going for now and look properly at the music therapy course for 2028, when I'd have the savings for it. I'd keep pushing the union campaign, because ten years is time to win something. I'd put off any big spending, like buying a flat with Jonas, until I could see where my income was heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe in this one. It feels like a long hill instead of a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put off buying a flat. How does Jonas feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He wants to buy in the next few years, and he's been patient. I'd tell him I want to see two years of my income holding up first. My partner Jonas wants a mortgage, and I want to know whether a violinist still has a job in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the slower timeline change whether you'd ever try AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. If the union won fair payment and the tools were properly licensed, I might use one to write out practice parts for students. But not for playing. I'd want my sound to be mine.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to fund teachers and pay artists fairly.
I'd push for **training payments** at the union and online.
think: Teaching and studio work likely gone by **2036**, when she's thirty-seven.
Weddings should last, giving room to train as a **music therapist**.
do: Keep **all current work** going while saving for a course.
Plan to start the **music therapy course** in 2028.
Delay **buying a flat** with Jonas until her income looks steady.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to breathe, like a **long hill** rather than a cliff.
S4.quote: My partner Jonas wants a mortgage, and I want to know whether a violinist still has a job in 2030.
fieldNote: Ten years turns panic into a **career plan**, but she still expects her main incomes to go.
The flat purchase is the first **household decision** she'd delay.
She'd only use AI under **union-licensed** terms and never for playing.

steps.text: Keep teaching at Mill Street and playing quartet weddings
Enrol in a part-time music therapy course in 2028
Delay buying a flat with Jonas for two years
Keep campaigning in the union for AI training payments

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, without question. There's no time to train or save, and I'd lose the teaching before I'd worked out what's next. What would help is a fund for musicians and teachers paid for by the companies, and a fee whenever our recordings train their programs. I've spent twenty years learning to make a violin sing, and nobody should be allowed to copy that for free.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids I teach. I worry about them more than me, honestly. If a nine-year-old learns violin only from a screen, nobody is there to notice when they're about to give up, and that's when a teacher matters most.

headlineQuote: I've spent twenty years learning to make a violin sing, and nobody should be allowed to copy that for free.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old violinist** who teaches, plays weddings with a quartet and takes occasional studio sessions.
She has about **three months** saved and splits rent with Jonas, a nurse, which she refuses to lean on.
A **union** loyalist, she won't touch AI tools and sees training on recordings as **taking work** without pay.
Her mood climbs from uneasy to **alarmed**, because teaching and studio work go first in the faster pictures.
With **ten years**, she'd slowly train as a music therapist and delay buying a flat.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd lose teaching before she could save or retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **fund** paid by AI companies for musicians and teachers, and a **fee** whenever recordings train AI.
